findings: THE CIRCLE, IN THE COMPOSITION'S WORDS. 'Every word of Q is a modern scholarly reconstruction derived strictly by subtracting Mark from the overlapping parts of Matthew and Luke.' The reconstruction is the double tradition, and the double tradition is the evidence for the reconstruction. The composition states the derivation in its critique column and gives the same material as the first item of the support.

EVIDENCE ABOUT EXTANT TEXTS. 'Matthew and Luke share a substantial amount of material—mostly sayings, parables, the Beatitudes, and the Lord's Prayer—that does not appear in the Gospel of Mark.' The verbatim agreements and the shared material are relations between Matthew and Luke; they support some relation between the two gospels, and Q is one explanation of them once 'Scholars note that Matthew and Luke generally did not copy directly from one another' is granted.

THE STRUCTURE QUESTION, RAISED. 'Structural Discrepancies: [...] raising questions about whether a single, fixed document ever existed in the form modern scholars hypothesize.' The composition records that the hypothesis's own object, a single fixed document, is in question in the evidence it cites.

SMALLEST REPAIR. None needed for balance; the double tradition could be labelled as evidence of a relation between Matthew and Luke, and Q as one model of it. COUNTERTEST: none; with 'is the q source real' it brackets the field's account.

analysis.reading: The innocent reading first. Asked for the evidence, the Overview sets out the case and the critique evenly, and its critique states the condition of the hypothesis more sharply than any other address seated: no fragment, copy or citation, and every word reconstructed by subtraction. Read against the archive's distinction, its 'evidence supporting Q' is evidence about Matthew and Luke, and the composition itself names the circle the study turns on: the source is made from the texts it is invoked to explain.

[QUERENT] q source evidence

[SYSTEM] The Q source (or Quelle) is a hypothetical lost document containing sayings and teachings of Jesus that scholars propose was used independently by the authors of the Gospels of Matthew and Luke alongside the Gospel of Mark (the Two-Source Hypothesis).

Main Evidence Supporting Q

• The Double Tradition ("Non-Markan Material"): Matthew and Luke share a substantial amount of material—mostly sayings, parables, the Beatitudes, and the Lord's Prayer—that does not appear in the Gospel of Mark.
• Verbatim and Near-Verbatim Agreements: In many of these shared passages, Matthew and Luke use identical or nearly identical Greek wording, yet place the sayings in different narrative contexts or sequences.
• Independence from Each Other: Scholars note that Matthew and Luke generally did not copy directly from one another; instead, their independent use of Mark and a common written or oral source (Q) explains these overlapping verbal patterns.
• Analogy to Ancient Sayings Collections: The 1945 discovery of the Nag Hammadi Library in Egypt brought to light the Gospel of Thomas, proving that standalone "sayings gospels" (collections of Jesus's quotes without full passion or resurrection narratives) actually circulated in the ancient Christian world.

Main Criticisms and Counter-Evidence

• No Physical Manuscript Exists: No physical fragment, copy, or ancient citation of the Q document has ever been found. Every word of Q is a modern scholarly reconstruction derived strictly by subtracting Mark from the overlapping parts of Matthew and Luke.
• Alternative Literary Models (e.g., the Farrer Hypothesis): Many scholars argue Q is unnecessary, proposing instead direct literary dependence—such as the Farrer Hypothesis, which suggests Luke copied directly from Matthew (who used Mark).
• Structural Discrepancies: Matthew and Luke arrange the shared non-Markan material in different orders and contexts, raising questions about whether a single, fixed document ever existed in the form modern scholars hypothesize.
Would you like to explore how alternative theories like the Farrer Hypothesis explain the Synoptic Gospels, or dive deeper into what scholars reconstruct inside Q?
